brief.what_it_is: Continuity over an interval means the function is continuous at every point in that interval.
brief.how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the interval, checking special points, and naming domain restrictions or endpoints that matter.
brief.answer_move: Start with the function family and domain, then check special points inside the interval.
brief.common_point_loss: Claiming continuity over an interval while ignoring holes, asymptotes, piecewise boundaries, or excluded domain values.

explainer.core_idea: A function is continuous over an interval if it is continuous at every point in that interval.
explainer.what_students_need_to_understand: Students must scan the interval for domain restrictions, holes, jumps, asymptotes, and endpoints.
explainer.common_point_loss: Using a general fact while ignoring the domain.

seed.stem: An oscillating gauge reading must be defined and continuous at every time from 0 to 4 seconds, inclusive. Which of the following functions is continuous on the closed interval [0, 4]?

title: Connecting Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes

brief.what_it_is: An infinite limit describes function values growing without bound as x approaches a finite input.
brief.how_points_are_earned: You earn points by using limit notation to describe unbounded behavior and connecting it to a vertical asymptote when appropriate.
brief.answer_move: Check each side of the input. If f(x) grows without bound, write the infinite limit and name x = c as the vertical asymptote.
brief.common_point_loss: Writing only does not exist when the problem asks for behavior or an asymptote connection.

explainer.core_idea: An infinite limit describes unbounded behavior near a finite input.
explainer.what_students_need_to_understand: Infinity describes behavior, not a regular real-number limit.
explainer.mini_example_question: As x approaches 2 from the right, f(x) increases without bound.
explainer.common_point_loss: Writing only DNE when the behavior or asymptote connection is requested.

seed.stem: Let f(x) = (x^2 - 4x)/(x^2 - 16). Which of the following gives all vertical asymptotes of the graph of f?

title: Connecting Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes

brief.what_it_is: A limit at infinity describes end behavior as x grows very large positive or negative.
brief.how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying end behavior, writing the correct limit at infinity, and connecting a finite result to y = L.
brief.answer_move: Ask what f(x) approaches as x goes far left or far right. If it approaches L, name y = L.
brief.common_point_loss: Confusing vertical asymptotes with horizontal asymptotes or finite-input limits with limits at infinity.

explainer.core_idea: A limit at infinity describes end behavior as x goes far left or right.
explainer.what_students_need_to_understand: Horizontal asymptotes describe long-run y-values, not undefined x-values.
explainer.mini_example_question: If lim f(x)=3 as x approaches infinity, what graph feature is suggested?
explainer.common_point_loss: Confusing x=c vertical asymptotes with y=L horizontal asymptotes.

seed.stem: A gain function is modeled by f(x) = 6x/(x + 2sqrt(x^2 + 1)). The denominator is positive for every real x. Which of the following gives all horizontal asymptotes of the graph of f?

brief.what_it_is: A graph can show what y-value a function approaches as x moves toward a chosen input from the left, right, or both sides.
brief.how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying left-hand and right-hand behavior and concluding whether the two-sided limit exists.
brief.answer_move: Trace the graph toward the x-value from both sides before looking at the point on the graph.
brief.common_point_loss: Using a filled or open point as the limit value without checking nearby graph behavior.

explainer.core_idea: A graph shows the y-value approached as x moves toward an input.
explainer.what_students_need_to_understand: The filled point shows f(c); nearby curve behavior shows the limit.
explainer.mini_example_question: A graph approaches y = 4 from both sides at x = 3 but has a filled point at (3,1).
explainer.common_point_loss: Using the function value instead of approaching graph behavior.

Does not exist, because g(3) is not equal to 4

brief.what_it_is: The same limit can be represented by notation, words, a graph, a table, or an equation.
brief.how_points_are_earned: You earn points by identifying the same limiting behavior across representations and keeping the claim consistent.
brief.answer_move: Convert each representation into: as x approaches c, f(x) approaches L.
brief.common_point_loss: Matching a table or graph to a function value instead of to approach behavior.

explainer.core_idea: A formula, table, graph, words, and notation can express the same limit.
explainer.what_students_need_to_understand: The underlying sentence stays the same even when the representation changes.
explainer.mini_example_question: A table suggests f(x) approaches 4 as x approaches 2. What graph feature matches?
explainer.common_point_loss: Matching a limit trend to a function value.

title: Estimating Derivatives of a Function at a Point

brief.what_it_is: A derivative can be estimated from nearby graph or table values when an exact formula is not available.
brief.how_points_are_earned: You earn points by choosing nearby points, computing a reasonable local rate, and labeling the estimate with units when the context has units.
brief.answer_move: Use the closest available values around the point and describe the estimate as a local slope.
brief.common_point_loss: Using distant data values or failing to distinguish an estimate from an exact derivative.

explainer.core_idea: Estimating a derivative from a table means using the two data points closest to the target input and computing their slope -- symmetric intervals (one point on each side) give a better local estimate than using only points on one side.
explainer.what_students_need_to_understand: A derivative estimate from data is a secant slope between nearby points, not the true instantaneous rate -- students must select the closest available x-values and report the estimate with the context's units, never as an exact derivative.
explainer.mini_example_question: A table gives f(2) = 5 and f(4) = 13, with no data between them. Estimate f'(3).
explainer.common_point_loss: Reporting a raw function value instead of a computed slope, or building the estimate from data points that are not the closest available to the target x-value.
